target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reduce school/work scheduling barriers and increase voting participation
objection: Declaring Election Day a federal holiday does not reliably reduce work-schedule barriers for private-sector hourly workers, because federal holiday status does not require private employers to close or provide paid leave; many retail and service workers would still be scheduled to work.

target: AG1’s claim that an Election Day holiday would not disadvantage low-income workers
objection: A federal Election Day holiday can disadvantage low-income workers because hourly retail and service employees are disproportionately low-income and may still have to work or lose wages, so the holiday can preserve time and pay pressure rather than relieve it.

target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would be effective at increasing turnout
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms, so the holiday is unlikely on its own to produce meaningful turnout gains.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not reduce work-schedule barriers because many employers stay open
objection: Many workplaces do observe federal holidays by closing or reducing operations, and placing Election Day on the federal holiday calendar would give employers and schools a day they already plan around, so the holiday would reduce work-schedule barriers for many hourly workers.

target: AG2’s claim that an Election Day holiday disadvantages low-income workers
objection: Reducing work-schedule barriers lowers the opportunity cost of voting, so a national holiday is not inherently harmful to low-income workers and can actually ease the wage/time pressure they face.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would not meaningfully improve voting because employers might still be open
objection: Even if some employers remain open, a national holiday can increase staffing and volunteer availability at polling places, which can reduce wait times and improve the feasibility of voting for workers with limited time.

target: AG2’s claim that treating Election Day as a holiday would not increase turnout without universal paid time off
objection: Making Election Day a civic celebration rather than a chore can itself increase people’s willingness to vote, so turnout can rise even without universal employer-paid leave.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is politically or practically weak because employer-paid leave is not guaranteed
objection: Broad bipartisan public support and the fact that many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays show the proposal is socially legitimate and internationally workable.

target: AG2’s claim that automatic voter registration or state employer time-off rules are better alternatives because they directly address voting barriers
objection: Those alternatives do not directly change school/work schedules on Election Day, which is the main barrier keeping many people from voting; a national holiday directly reduces that day-specific scheduling conflict.

target: AG2’s claim that civic celebration framing is insufficient to matter
objection: A public holiday creates a widely visible social norm and expectation that voting is what people should do that day, which can motivate participation even without guaranteed paid leave.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reliably reduces practical voting barriers for shift workers
objection: A holiday mostly addresses day-specific schedule constraints, but it does not change voters’ registration or eligibility status, so it leaves an important turnout barrier untouched.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday is a reliable access reform
objection: Compared with reforms that target both scheduling and registration barriers, a holiday is less reliable because it addresses only one barrier type and does not eliminate administrative obstacles to voting.

target: AG1’s claim that low-income workers would benefit from the holiday
objection: Low-income workers may be less able to turn a calendar holiday into actual voting time because they have rigid, low-flexibility work arrangements, so the holiday can still disadvantage them relative to higher-income workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reduce voting barriers by giving people more time
objection: If the holiday increases turnout without proportional polling-place capacity, it can raise wait times, which increases time pressure and can especially burden low-income workers.

target: AG1’s claim that federal holiday status will reduce work barriers for private-sector workers
objection: Federal law does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off on federal holidays, so many retail and service workplaces would still remain open and keep workers on the schedule.

target: AG2’s claim that local school and childcare schedules would not change on Election Day if it were a federal holiday
objection: A national holiday would change school, childcare, and workplace scheduling routines for that day, reducing day-of coordination conflicts that keep many people from voting.

target: AG1’s claim that school and childcare conflicts would reliably ease if Election Day were a holiday
objection: School district calendars and childcare provider routines are local and are not compelled to change just because Election Day is a federal holiday, so the holiday would not reliably alter childcare availability across communities.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reliably reduce practical day-of barriers for parents and caregivers
objection: Because school and childcare coverage windows would not consistently shift, a federal holiday cannot be counted on to reliably reduce practical day-of scheduling conflicts for voters who depend on those routines.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reliably solve voting-access problems
objection: Election-day feasibility also depends on polling-place staffing, location availability, and wait times, and a federal holiday does not itself require officials to extend hours or add sites, so practical access barriers can remain.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday would reliably help shift workers
objection: For fixed shift workers, a federal holiday does not automatically change shift schedules or guarantee paid time off to vote, so it does not reliably expand the usable voting window they need.

target: AG1’s claim that low-income workers are not inherently disadvantaged by the holiday
objection: Because low-income workers are more likely to be stuck in rigid hourly shifts and cannot easily swap shifts or take unpaid time, the holiday may leave them disadvantaged in practice instead of solving their access problem.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reduce travel-related barriers to voting
objection: Election Day holidays can coincide with reduced public transit service, and low-income voters are more likely to rely on transit, so the holiday can increase travel time or uncertainty about reaching the polls rather than lowering it.
